## Purpose and completion criteria

Assess a switch to allow multiple group columns to a simulation to allow more than one group designation within the same simulation.

| Measure | Comparison | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Accounting and implementation | Existing tests | Successful unit tests |

## Overview of Design

The `group` column is intended to be abstract so that users can use it for different kinds of things. For example, it could designate ethnoracial groups, educational categories, or regions. While this is useful, users are still limited to a single group column. So, if they want a simulation that includes both regional migration and ethnoracial breakdowns, they will have a difficult time. While it is possible to hack together a set of categories for a group that are a combination of multiple groups that the user wants, this is not easy or elegant.

However, we have all the internal plumbing to allow for more than one group. Its really just another stratification dimension and we know how to handle those already. So, while it will takes some work to update the code to accept multiple group columns, it doesn't require any big underlying changes to the engine. The biggest change is to the calibration method for group weighting used for intergroup partnership, which I discuss below.

To allow for multiple groups, we have created a separate `set_groups` argument for building the model. This is a change from the program inferring groups from the `group` column. Now, users can use any name they want to identify a group column (e.g. race, region, education) and then explicitly define it as a group column with the `group()` function. The inheritance model also now belongs to this `group()` output. Users can also specify explicit categories for the group in `group` rather than in the inheritance model, but if they don't, categories will be inferred from the data. So, here is an example setup:

```r
model |>
  set_groups(
   race = group(
      categories = c("white", "black", "other"),
      ancestry = TRUE,
      inheritance = create_group_inheritance("random_parent")
    ),
   region = group(
      categories = c("NE", "MW", "S", "W"),
      ancestry = FALSE,
      inheritance = create_group_inheritance("mother")
    )
  )
```

Group exogamy parameters still live in the matching model but are now specified with a named list structure where names identify which group's exogamy is being considered. So:

```r
model |>
  set_union_formation(
    "on_demand", 
    matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(
      2, 5,
      group_exogamy = list(
        race = c("white:black" = -4, "white:other" = -2, "black:other" = -3),
        region = NA
      )
    )
  )
```

This will allow for exogamy rates between each of the three racial groups, while no exogamy will be allowed between regions.

Transition rate schedules will now apply to specific groups with the `group` argument. `'group_origin` and `group_dest` have been replaced with `origin` and `destination`. The transition rates for one group can be stratified by other groups. So, for example, you could stratify educational transitions to be different by region. Here is an example of how you would set a rate schedule for a specific group:

```r
model |>
  set_group_transition(educ_trans_rates, group = "education")
```

This would set the transition rates for the education group.

### Changes to helpers

Because of the new structure, we have removed all of the `group_prop_hazard` arguments from the rate processes. Instead, we create a `stratify_rates` function that takes an existing rate object and stratifies it by additional variables using proportional hazards. This can be used for any stratification variable of the user's choice, so it allows users to quickly build up a stratified rate schedule from an initial schedule.

We also adjusted the `calculate_*_rates` functions to take a single `by` argument as a character vector rather than the various boolean by_* that were used across different functions. This allows more flexibility in how users can stratify the lexis counts they desire and makes it easy to inlude group columns that have unique names.

## Stratifying Rates

We show some examples here of how you can use `stratify_rates` to stratify rates. In the first example, I will take a fertility schedule from the Human Fertility Database and then statify two groups A and B and by union type for unpartnered/partnered.

```{r}
#| label: stratify-fert-union-type

fertility_rates <- get_fertility_hfd("USA", 2000)

fertility_rates <- stratify_rates(
  fertility_rates, 
  by = list(
    group = c(A = 1.1, B = 1),
    # this is not really a great idea for union type as within union
    # type fertility rates have a totally different age profile, but 
    # ok for testing purposes
    union_type = c("unpartnered" = 0.3, "partnered" = 1.3)
  )
)

fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()
```

This approach will work, but this is not the best use of proportional hazards. We know that the age-specific profile of fertility *within* unions is very different than the overall age-specific fertility profile, so the proportional hazards approach will give us some unusual fertility distributions. A better approach would be to start with pre-stratified fertility rates by union type drawn from real data and then apply proportional hazards by group to that data, as I do in the second example.


```{r}
#| label: stratify-pre-strat-fert-by-group

fertility_rates_by_union_type <- read_csv(
  here(
  "validation", "data", "usa_2000_2001", "usa_2000_fertility_by_union_status.csv"
  )
) |>
  rename(union_type = union_status)
fertility_rates <- stratify_rates(
  fertility_rates_by_union_type,
  by = list(group = c(A = 1.1, B = 1))
)
fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()
```

If we want to relax, the proportional hazards assumption, we could break up the fertility rates by union type, statify with different ratios, and then combine them back together. In the example below, we make the ratio between A and B 1.05 for partnered fertility but 1.2 for unpartnered fertility.

```{r}
#| label: stratify-fert-non-proportional

fertility_rates <- bind_rows(
  fertility_rates_by_union_type |>
    filter(union_type == "partnered") |>
    stratify_rates(list(group = c(A = 1.05, B = 1))),
  fertility_rates_by_union_type |>
    filter(union_type == "unpartnered") |>
    stratify_rates(list(group = c(A = 1.20, B = 1)))
)
fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()
```


## Race-Region Simulation

To test out the new capabilities, lets create a simulation with three racial groups (W, B, and O) and four regional groups (NE, MW, S, W). We will allow exogamy between racial groups but will not allow exogamy by region (because marriage markets are generally local).

For this simulation, we will use a rate model for union formation and allow fertility vary by union type, but we won't add the complication of cohabitation. We will also stratify all input rats across group dimensions.

### Fertility inputs

We will use 2000 US fertility rates split by partnered status. We will apply proportional hazards by region, but allow the hazards to vary by union type for race.

```{r}
#| label: set-fertility-rate


fertility_rates_by_union_type <- read_csv(
  here(
  "validation", "data", "usa_2000_2001", "usa_2000_fertility_by_union_status.csv"
  )
) |>
  rename(union_type = union_status)


fertility_rates <- bind_rows(
  fertility_rates_by_union_type |>
    filter(union_type == "partnered") |>
    stratify_rates(list(race = c(W = 1, B = 1.05, O = 1.05))),
  fertility_rates_by_union_type |>
    filter(union_type == "unpartnered") |>
    stratify_rates(list(race = c(W = 1, B = 1.2, O = 1.05)))
) |>
  stratify_rates(list(region = c(NE = 1, MW = 1.05, S = 1.1, W = 1)))

fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()
```

### Mortality inputs

We use 2000 US mortality rates, truncated at 95. We allow these to vary by region and race slightly

```{r}
# label: set-mortality-rates

mortality_rates <- get_mortality_hmd("USA", 2000, open_age = 95)

mortality_rates <- mortality_rates |> stratify_rates(
  list(race = c(W = 0.97, B =1.07, O = 1), region = c(NE = 1, MW = 1, S = 1.05, W = 0.96))
)

mortality_rates |> calculate_life_table() |>
  filter(age_start == 0) |>
  select(race, region, sex, ex)
```

### Marriage inputs

We will use a single set of marriage rates drawn from the US 2000-2001. I will allow these to vary by race as well, but we will use weight models to accomplish that so that the overall marriage rates are preserved in the simulation 

```{r}
#| label: set-mar-rates

marriage_rates <- read_csv(
  here("validation", "data", "usa_2000_2001", "usa_2001_marriage_rates_female.csv")
)
```

### Migration inputs

In terms of transition rates, we will not allow any transitions between racial groups, but we will allow transitions between regions which indicates internal migration rates. We use reprorts from US Census 2000 to construct plausible age-specific migration rates.

**TODO:** For now individuals migrate, but this obviously causes problems for married couples and their children. We will add household level moves in a later feature and when we do we will need to adjust these rates to avoid double jeopardy  - If you can move when your partner/parent/child moves then overall migration rates will be overstated. The easiest way to do this would be to set moving under a certain age to zero so that it needs to be sparked by parents and set one sex to zero or halve the rates.

```{r}
#| label: set-migration-rates

migration_rates <- read_csv("validation/data/usa_2000_2001/usa_2000_regional_migration.csv")
```



### Running the model

For the starter population, I want to start with uneven weights by race-region combination, so I will first set up that joint distribution. Values are loosely modeled on US 2000 racial distributions by race.

```{r}
region_race_dist <- tribble(
  ~race, ~region, ~weight,
  "W",   "NE",    0.145,
  "W",   "MW",    0.190,
  "W",   "S",     0.257,
  "W",   "W",     0.152,
  "B",   "NE",    0.022,
  "B",   "MW",    0.023,
  "B",   "S",     0.067,
  "B",   "W",     0.019,
  "O",   "NE",    0.021,
  "O",   "MW",    0.014,
  "O",   "S",     0.030,
  "O",   "W",     0.060,
)
sum(region_race_dist$weight)
```

Now lets create the starter population.

```{r}
#| label: create-starter-pop

set.seed(42)
pop_start <- create_baseline_population(100000, groups = region_race_dist)
```

Now we are ready to set up the model.

```{r}


model <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(pop_start) |>
  set_fertility(fertility_rates) |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates) |>
  set_union_formation(
    "rate", 
    rates = marriage_rates,
    matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(
      2, 5,
      group_exogamy = list(
        race = c("W:B" = -4, "W:O" = -2, "B:O" = -3),
        # marriage markets are local so no cross-region marriages
        region = NA
      )
    ),
    # make B group have marriage rates 10% lower than other groups
    weights = create_weight_model(~ race, c(raceB = log(0.9), raceO = 0))
  ) |>
  set_groups(
    # we don't need to set categories here because they are defined from the population
    race = group(ancestry = TRUE, inheritance = "ancestry"),
    region = group(inheritance = "mother")
  ) |>
  set_group_transition(migration_rates, group = "region", household = household())

system.time(pop_end <- simulate(model, 100, 42))
```

```{r}
calculate_population_size(pop_end, seq(0, 100, 5), by = c("race")) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  mutate(prop = population / sum(population)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop, group = race, fill = race))+
  geom_area()
```

```{r}

calculate_population_size(pop_end, seq(0, 100, 5), by = c("region")) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  mutate(prop = population / sum(population)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop, group = region, fill = region))+
  geom_area()
```

```{r}

calculate_population_size(pop_end, seq(0, 100, 5), by = c("region")) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  mutate(prop = population / sum(population)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = prop, group = region, color = region))+
  geom_line()+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA))
```

What else?

- check intermarriage rates
- check fertility rates, mortality rates, and marriage rates by group and region and overall
- check transition rates. They should match for women over age 18.

```{r}
calculate_fertility_rates(
  pop_end,
  time_breaks = c(0, 100),
  age_breaks = seq(15, 45, 5),
  by = c("union_type", "race", "region"),
  conf.level = 0.95
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start, y = rate_fertility, color = union_type))+

```

```{r}
calculate_mortality_rates(
  pop_end,
  time_breaks = c(0, 100),
  age_breaks = 50:95,

) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start, y = rate_mortality, color = sex))+

  geom_point(size = 0.5)+

```

```{r}
calculate_marriage_rates(
  pop_end,
  time_breaks = c(0, 100),
  age_breaks = seq(15, 70, 5),
  conf.level = 0.95
) |>
  filter(sex == "f") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start, y = rate_marriage))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf_low, ymax = conf_high), fill = "grey60", color = NA, alpha = 0.3)+
  geom_point(size = 0.5)+
  geom_line(data = marriage_rates, aes(y = rate), linetype = 2)
```

```{r}
df_hazard <- calculate_marriage_rates(
  pop_end,
  time_breaks = c(25, 100),
  age_breaks = seq(15, 70, 5),
  by = "race"
) |>
  filter(sex == "f") |>
  mutate(group_b = race == "B")

model <- glm(marriages ~ factor(age_start) + group_b + offset(log(person_years)), 
             family = poisson, data = df_hazard)

modelsummary(
  list("exp(beta)" = model),
  out = "gt",
  coef_map = c("group_bTRUE" = "Group B"),
  statistic = "conf.int",
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  gof_map = c("nobs"), 
  notes = "Note: Model also includes age group dummies"
)
```

Show that no marriages occurred across regions.

```{r}
pop_end |>
  get_detailed_unions() |>
  count(region_w, region_h)
```


```{r}

expected <- tibble(
  pair = c("W:B", "W:O", "B:O"),
  expected = c(-4, -2, -3) * 2
)

pop_end |>
  get_detailed_unions() |>
  #filter(start_time > 25) |>
  count(race_w, race_h) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(race_w, race_h), values_from = n) |>
  mutate(
    log_odds_W_B = log(W_B) + log(B_W) - log(W_W) - log(B_B),
    se_W_B = sqrt(1 / W_B + 1 / B_W + 1 / W_W + 1 / B_B),
    log_odds_W_O = log(W_O) + log(O_W) - log(W_W) - log(O_O),
    se_W_O = sqrt(1 / W_O + 1 / O_W + 1 / W_W + 1 / O_O),
    log_odds_B_O = log(B_O) + log(O_B) - log(B_B) - log(O_O),
    se_B_O = sqrt(1 / B_O + 1 / O_B + 1 / B_B + 1 / O_O)
  ) |>
  select(starts_with("log_odds"), starts_with("se_")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c(".value", "pair"),
    names_pattern = "(log_odds|se)_(.*)"
  ) |>
  mutate(pair = str_replace(pair, "_", ":")) |>
  left_join(expected, by = "pair") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pair, y = log_odds))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = log_odds - 1.96 * se, ymax = log_odds + 1.96 * se))+
  geom_point(aes(y = expected), color = "red", alpha = 0.7)+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(x = "interracial pairing", y = "log-odds")
```


## Unit Tests

The following tests have been constructed and are currently all passing.

```{r}
#| label: test-results
#| eval: true

test_results <- devtools::test(pkg = here::here(), reporter = "silent")
test_table <- as.data.frame(test_results)
knitr::kable(
  test_table[, c("test", "passed", "failed", "error", "skipped", "warning")]
)
```
## Conclusions and Unresolved Limitations

This milestone meets all expectation. The new approach to producing events is working as expected and continues to preserve input rates in the output. The new approach increases runtime slightly in some situations but reduces it in other situations. The weight models are producing the expected proportional hazards in the output.

Remaining limitations include the fact that weights may fail to produce expected difference when bins are sparsely populated and the continued issue of unrealized births in sparse bins.
